edition: Brené Brown, Dare to Lead, Random House, 2018; author-site article adapted from the book, 15 October 2018
exact_text: Clear is kind. Unclear is unkind.
surrounding_context: Brown describes how avoiding difficult conversations damages trust, behavior, performance, and clarity. She then states the principle, explains that she first encountered the saying roughly two decades earlier at a 12-step meeting, and connects it to her research.
locator: Author article adapted from Dare to Lead
notes: Author's own site labels the article as adapted from Dare to Lead. Confirms both the wording and the 12-step-meeting provenance. The 2018 physical book was not separately inspected.

edition: George Long, trans., George Bell and Sons, 1877
exact_text: it is impossible that a man can keep company with one who is covered with soot without being partaker of the soot himself.
surrounding_context: Immediately before, Long gives the image of quenched charcoal placed beside burning charcoal. Epictetus then warns about intimate association with ordinary company and follows with examples involving gladiators, horses, athletes, and gossip.
notes: Charcoal and soot image present in Long. Inspected edition names Long as translator, George Bell and Sons, 1877. Suitable for the house Long standard.

edition: Elizabeth Carter, trans., Hulton Bradley, Dublin, 1759; compared with George Long, 1877
exact_text: In our Power are Opinion, Pursuit, Desire, Aversion, and in one Word, whatever are our own Actions.
surrounding_context: Carter opens by dividing things into those in our power and those not in our power. She lists body, property, reputation, and command among the latter, then describes things in our power as naturally free, unrestrained, and unhindered.
notes: NEEDS CORRECTION BEFORE PRINT. The wording in the manuscript is displayed by MIT Classics under Carter's name but is NOT the verbatim wording of the 1759 Carter edition. Carter uses Power rather than control and preserves 18th-century capitalization. Long 1877 also differs substantially, beginning 'Of things some are in our power'. The current quote cannot accurately be labeled verbatim Carter 1759.

edition: George Long, trans., George Bell and Sons, 1877; compared with Carter 1759
exact_text: Duties are universally measured by relations (ταῖς σχέσεσι).
surrounding_context: Epictetus immediately applies the principle to a father, including care, yielding, and accepting correction. He then considers a brother who does wrong and instructs the reader to preserve his own proper position rather than making his conduct dependent on the brother's behavior.
notes: Source and central claim confirmed in Long 1877. Carter 1759 begins the chapter with the same proposition but capitalizes Relations and diverges after. For a verbatim quotation use one translation consistently rather than combining sentences.

edition: George Long, trans., George Bell and Sons, 1877; compared with Matheson 1916 and Oldfather (Loeb) 1928
exact_text: Immediately prescribe some character and some form to yourself, which you shall observe both when you are alone and when you meet with men.
surrounding_context: Opening of chapter 33. Epictetus proceeds to rules concerning silence, speaking only when necessary, avoiding commonplace conversation, moderating laughter, refusing oaths when possible, and disciplined behavior in company.
notes: Long 1877 confirms the wording exactly. CORRECTION TO OUR NOTES: Matheson 1916 does NOT use the 'Immediately prescribe' wording; Matheson begins 'Lay down for yourself from the first' and speaks of a definite stamp and style of conduct. Oldfather 1928 likewise begins 'Lay down for yourself, at the outset'. The passage is genuine but our Matheson attribution was incorrect.

edition: George Long, trans., George Bell and Sons, 1877; compared with Carter 1759
exact_text: Seek not that the things which happen should happen as you wish; but wish the things which happen to be as they are
surrounding_context: The sentence stands alone as chapter 8 and concludes by promising a tranquil flow of life. Chapter 7 before it uses the ship, captain, shellfish, wife, and child analogy; chapter 9 after distinguishes bodily impediments from impediments to the will.
notes: Complete wording confirmed in Long's 1877 edition including the tranquil-flow phrase. The 1888 date we recorded was NOT verified; the edition actually inspected is George Bell and Sons, 1877. Carter 1759 is materially different and the MIT Carter page modernizes further. Use the verified 1877 attribution.

edition: Gregory Hays, trans., Modern Library, 2002; compared with George Long, Little Brown, 1889
exact_text: Everything that happens is either endurable or not. If it's endurable, then endure it. Stop complaining.
surrounding_context: Section 3 of Book 10. The preceding section tells the reader to follow the demands of rational and civic nature. The remainder of section 3 addresses what happens when something is unendurable and the mind's ability to make experiences endurable.
notes: Hays wording matches a full-text reproduction of the Modern Library edition. Google Play independently confirms Hays as translator, Modern Library, May 2002. The passage was NOT exposed in the official publisher/Google preview, so inspection relied on a third-party reproduction rather than an official scan. IMPORTANT: Long 1889 expresses the same argument in markedly different language, beginning with what a person is formed by nature to bear.

edition: A. S. L. Farquharson, trans. and ed., Clarendon Press, 1944; compared with Long 1889
exact_text: but if what is wrong, clearly they act involuntarily and in ignorance—for as every soul is unwilling to be deprived of the truth
surrounding_context: Third item in Marcus's sequence of reminders for dealing with other people. He first considers humanity's social relationship, then the constraints created by people's opinions. After this statement he notes their resentment at being characterized as unjust or inconsiderate.
notes: NEEDS CORRECTION BEFORE PRINT. Not verbatim Farquharson. The 1944 text reads 'but if what is wrong', not 'if they do what is wrong'. The remainder of the clause is substantially correct, and the em dash after ignorance IS genuine to Farquharson's printed wording. Long 1889 differs again.
